This attribute is advantageous in limited resource settings where thorough testing of foods should be done, although it may be rather cumbersome (Trinh et al., 2023).

Taken together, these advantages indicate that microfluidics is particularly suited to screening and preliminary authentication where rapid decision-making is required. Nevertheless, portability and low sample volume should not be considered substitutes for analytical validation. For practical adoption, sensitivity, selectivity, reproducibility, matrix tolerance, and operator-independent interpretation must be demonstrated alongside portability and low cost.
Lab-on-a-chip technology miniaturizes all laboratory operations into a single chip for enhanced portability and automation (Whitesides, 2006b).

Recent advancements comprise the application of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning in real-time analysis of data that enhances sensitivity and accuracy for the detection of fraudulent foods. Microfluidic PCR and immunoassays have been incorporated into LOC systems to enable better detection of pathogens and contaminants in field-deployable and on-site applications (Nguyen et al., 2019).

Microfluidic electrochemical sensors offer high selectivity, sensitivity, and in situ monitoring capabilities (Nguyen et al., 2019). Microfluidic electrochemical sensors have been widely used for the detection of heavy metal impurities in seafood, food additives of synthetic dyes, and artificial sweeteners in processed foods.

The combination of microfluidics and smartphones provides real-time analysis and data acquisition, improving user convenience and access to food fraud detection (Xu et al., 2020). Microfluidic-based smartphone systems have been employed for the successful analysis of food colorants, verification of organic food labeling, and the detection of food fraud. Smartphone integration can support image-based readout, portable data acquisition, and remote recording of test results, thereby facilitating field-level food analysis.

sections.title: Case study: real-world examples of food fraud detection and prevention

paragraphs.en: The following case studies provide study-specific evidence of the analytical performance and practical application of food-fraud detection technologies, with emphasis on reported detection limits, accuracy, response time, and portability.

In many developing countries, including India, Pakistan, and China, the addition of adulterants such as urea, detergent, and hydrogen peroxide to milk is a serious health concern. As a solution to this challenge, Subhashis Patari et al. (2022) designed a novel three-dimensional paper-based microfluidic system that can detect seven different adulterants with fast color changes in 1–2 mL of milk withina few minutes. This portable system has a detection limit of 0.05%–0.2% with a recovery percentage of 85%–107%. In comparison to other techniques like HPLC and mass spectrometry, the cost-effective nature of this microdevice makes it an ideal choice for detection. It took less than 30 s to provide test results than other laboratory methods.

Additional advancements in milk authentication include:•PCR-based methods detecting buffalo, goat, and sheep milk mixed with cow milk (Giglioti et al., 2022).•Laser-Induced Breakdown Spectroscopy (LIBS) identifying bovine milk adulteration with caprine and ovine milk (Sezer et al., 2018).•Smartphone-integrated digital colorimetry identifying water dilution in milk (Silva & Rocha, 2020).
PCR-based methods detecting buffalo, goat, and sheep milk mixed with cow milk (Giglioti et al., 2022).
Laser-Induced Breakdown Spectroscopy (LIBS) identifying bovine milk adulteration with caprine and ovine milk (Sezer et al., 2018).
Smartphone-integrated digital colorimetry identifying water dilution in milk (Silva & Rocha, 2020).

sections.title: Detection of aflatoxin M1 and other contaminants

paragraphs.en: A portable and cost-effective paper-based microfluidic device (μPAD), which uses AuNPs, has been designed by Kasoju et al. (2020) for the detection of Aflatoxin M1, a milk contaminant associated with liver damage and cancer. While techniques such as HPLC and ELISA are quite costly and require a lot of time, this μPAD changes its color from red to blue upon detecting Aflatoxin M1. This μPAD has a detection limit of 3 pM in water and 10 nM in milk, lasts up to three months, and is best suited for field tests.

Likewise, Selvaraj and Ravi Shankaran (2023) developed a nano-enabled plasmonic μPAD for melamine detection, with the change in color from orange-red to purple indicating contamination at a 5.0 × 10−5 M detection limit. Moreover, Ray, Prabhu, Prasad, Garlapati, et al. (2022) and Ray, Prabhu, Prasad, kumar Garlapati, et al. (2022) developed a wax-printed μPAD for starch adulteration by using the iodine-starch colorimetric reaction, and its detection limit is 0.05%.

The problem of milk fraud, such as misleading labeling of UHT milk as fresh and manipulation of fat content, is becoming more prevalent in the dairy industry. In this study, Field Flow Fractionation (FFF) along with chemometrics was employed for the analysis of 47 milk samples, allowing differentiation between UHT and non-UHT milk due to the detection of heat-induced changes in protein aggregation. This technique allowed tracing milk back to the manufacturing plant, which in turn demonstrated that various milk brands usually come from the same production site. Moreover, milk was classified based on fat content (whole, semi-skimmed, skimmed). This technique proved to be superior to the conventional Gerber method of fat content estimation. As compared to common HPLC and NMR techniques, this technique does not require any organic solvents and allows analysis of samples in less than an hour (Giordani et al., 2024).

Honey adulteration, which involves mixing glucose syrup with honey, can be easily detected by the use of a sensitive amperometric biosensor that is coupled to the screen-printed carbon electrode (SPCE). In spite of being very sensitive, stability of the biosensor is only achieved for five days, making the biosensor appropriate for immediate analysis (Julika et al., 2020).

Biswas & Chaudhari, 2024 note that NIR spectroscopy is the most appropriate method to detect honey adulterants such as high-fructose corn syrup (HFCS), where 98.7% accuracy can be achieved (Bázár et al., 2016). The use of machine learning approaches, such as SVM and ANN, further improves accuracy (Benković et al., 2022).

sections.title: Microfluidic detection in food fraud prevention

paragraphs.en: Adulteration of EGGs: A novel technique for detection of tea-coated broiler eggs passed off as country eggs is introduced by Ray et al. (2023a, 2023b). The test makes use of paper-based microfluidic devices wherein ferric chloride (FeCl₃) is used to develop a dark blue precipitate with tea polyphenols, while citric acid is used to remove the stain and reveal the white color of the eggshell. An automated AI-based application named “Eggo” can detect these with 100% accuracy within five minutes. The chemical reactions have been validated by FTIR spectroscopy; out of six field samples tested in Karnataka, only one was found to be a fake one.

Detection of essential oils: Essential oils (EOs) are frequently used in food, cosmetics, and medical applications. However, the volatile nature and demands of the market make them prone to adulteration. The review by Yang et al. (2024) examines the use of sensory evaluation, physicochemical characteristics, and chemical composition analysis as crucial methods of authentication. The sensory evaluation, which involves both a human sensory panel and technology-based sensors, distinguishes between authentic and adulterated products by using odor and texture properties. The physicochemical analysis involves the evaluation of density, refractive index, optical rotation, and acid and ester value, with any difference indicating the presence of potential adulteration. Chemical analysis identifies significant compounds such as terpenes and aldehydes and changes due to oxidation and fraudulent activities.

The adulteration of cooking oil, in particular the mixing of cheap oils such as palm oil with premium oils like sunflower oil, was successfully detected using μPAD assays. The detection of palm oil in sunflower oil was done using μPAD analysis, which involved analysis of the greyscale intensity of the sample, revealing a linear relationship within the 10–50% level (Muthukumar et al., 2021). Adulteration of cow ghee with both palm oil and sunflower oil was conducted through the μPAD that was impregnated with 2,2-Diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) as a color indicator, detecting 2.5% palm oil and 1% sunflower oil levels (Naik et al., 2023).

This case serves to emphasize an important benefit of using μPAD technology: the possibility of transforming the relatively complicated task of adulteration into a fast screening method. Nevertheless, it would be important to test the applicability of these tests for different types of oil, different types of adulterants, and different concentrations because food matrices might have an impact on assay reaction.

The case studies presented above demonstrate a common trend toward moving from laboratory detection to portable testing. Nevertheless, the performance of each particular device is usually evaluated on the basis of certain experimental conditions and food matrices. Therefore, the main challenge now is not limited to the development of sensitive microfluidic methods anymore. It is necessary to validate these tests.

sections.title: Functional food and dairy fraud detection

paragraphs.en: The Nanjing Institute for Food and Drug Control and the National Institute of Metrology in China conducted a study on illicit pharmaceutical additives in functional foods using the MRSIT-HRMS (Multiple Sample Rapid Introduction combined with High Resolution Mass Spectrometry) technology, a rapid screening method that does not require chromatography. Researchers tested 50 batches from the Nanjing Municipal Public Security Bureau and discovered 41 samples that were heavily contaminated with sildenafil, tadalafil, sibutramine, ephedrine, and furosemide, all of which are used to treat erectile dysfunction, lose weight, and regulate blood pressure. The technique achieved 100% accuracy, which is comparable to the reliability of LC-MS/MS (Hu, Zou, et al., 2024b).

Traditional authentication techniques, such as chemical tests and NIR spectroscopy, struggle to detect quality differences in Parmigiano Reggiano cheese. Becchi et al. (2024a, 2024b) utilized untargeted metabolomics (UHPLC-MS) and machine learning to identify markers linked to ripening, altitude, and rind inclusion. The model achieved over 60% accuracy in detecting excessive rind content (>18%).

Pomegranate juice adulteration: Hu and Lu (2020a) at the University of British Columbia in Canada developed a low-cost, portable Lab-on-a-Chip that detects pomegranate juice contamination by cheaper juices such as apple and grape. Fresh juices were stored at −20 °C, while counterfeit samples were produced in 1:1 and 1:1:1 ratios. Two DNA extraction methods were evaluated: the Qiagen DNeasy Kit and the Fusion 5 paper-based method. LAMP primers were used to target species-specific DNA (matK for grape, ITS for apple and pomegranate) at 63 °C for 45 min. The LOC device included seven layers and contained a Fusion 5 DNA extraction zone, microfluidic flow channels, and a portable heater. A fluorometric dye system detected positive samples (green under UV light) and negative samples (black), and the results were recorded on an iPhone 6.

The gadget detected pomegranate DNA at 10 pg and grape/apple DNA at 100 pg, with a limit of detection (LOD) of 2 μL for pomegranate and 5 μL for apple/grape. The authentication process was speedy (∼1 h), reliable, and field-ready, with a cost of $4 per test. The study established LOC-LAMP technology as a viable approach for detecting food theft, benefiting regulators, manufacturers, and inspectors. Future improvements include larger DNA databases and smartphone-based result interpretation.

Wine adulteration: Smartphone-based digital image analysis is a more cost-effective and practical way to examine the authenticity of Slovak Tokaj wine compared to traditional methods. Researchers evaluated 63 wine samples (41 from Slovakia and 22 from other locations) with a Samsung Galaxy S8 in a customised cubic cage with controlled luminance. MATLAB was used to process photos and generate histograms in greyscale, RGB, and HSV. Three chemometric models were investigated, including OC-PLS, DD-SIMCA, and PLS-DM. DD-SIMCA and PLS-DM reached 100% accuracy; however, OC-PLS had lower specificity (65%). Chemometric modelling using smartphone pictures is a cost-effective and efficient way to authenticate wine and prevent fraud (Onça et al., 2024).

The pomegranate juice study illustrates how molecular amplification can be integrated with a portable microfluidic platform to achieve species-specific authentication outside conventional laboratory settings. At the same time, the requirement for target-specific primers indicates that such systems are better suited to predefined fraud scenarios than to broad, non-targeted screening. Expansion of target databases and multiplexed assays could therefore improve their applicability to more complex adulteration patterns.

Whisky dilution and caramel addition can be identified using redox titration-based μPADs (Rezende et al., 2022). More concerning is the fraudulent addition of paracetamol (PAR) in whisky. Moreira et al. (2024) designed a distance-based μPAD that detects PAR through a Prussian blue reaction, with a detection range of 15–120 mg/L.

Tuna fish: Food fraud in the tuna sector is a major concern due to the economic worth and price disparities across species, which lead to mislabelling and substitution. Traditional morphological identification is useless for processed tuna, while DNA-based approaches are prone to degradation. This work used metabolomics-based mass spectrometry to distinguish between skipjack tuna (Katsuwonus pelamis), bigeye tuna (Thunnus obesus), and yellowfin tuna (Thunnus albacares) utilising UPLC-Q/Orbitrap MS for non-volatile metabolites and GC-Q-TOFMS for volatile metabolites. Tuna samples from the Indian Ocean were held at −60 °C, crushed in liquid nitrogen, and extracted with a mixture of acetonitrile, methanol, and water (2:2:1, v/v/v). A total of 77 metabolites (UPLC-MS) and 22 metabolites (GC–MS) were discovered, with 38 biomarkers differentiated using PCA and OPLS-DA, and verified using Hierarchical Cluster Analysis (HCA) and heat maps. Bigeye and yellowfin tuna displayed comparable profiles; however, skipjack tuna had different amino acid and lipid compositions. KEGG pathway enrichment revealed 27 metabolic pathways, such as glutamine metabolism, phenylalanine biosynthesis, and fatty acid metabolism. This work indicates that metabolomics-based authentication is a useful technique for detecting tuna fraud, providing regulatory bodies, seafood traders, and consumers with accurate species discrimination. (Hu, Zhu, et al., 2024).

Meat adulteration, particularly the mislabeling of pork as halal meat, was identified using a hybrid μPAD combined with solid-phase extraction. DNA fragments were selectively captured using polydopamine-modified magnetic nanoparticles and analyzed via colorimetric detection, achieving a detection limit of 4.59 nmol/mL. This method provides a reliable solution for ensuring halal food authenticity and preventing religious and ethical fraud.

sections.title: Challenges and limitations in current food fraud detection practices

paragraphs.en: Advances in food fraud detection have resulted in tremendous gains, but numerous hurdles remain, impeding their effectiveness and widespread use. These limits are due to the complexity of food matrices, technological constraints, regulatory gaps, and hurdles to industrial integration. Addressing these problems is critical for improving detection accuracy, assuring regulatory compliance, and facilitating real-world application.1.Matrix complexity and interference issues: Many detection techniques are challenging to use because food matrices are complex and contain a variety of physical and chemical components that can interfere with analytical results. Microfluidic paper-based analytical devices (μPADs) have limited sensitivity and specificity for identifying adulterants in dairy, honey, and culinary oils due to matrix effects.2.Limited multi-analyte detection capabilities: While classic techniques such as HPLC and GC–MS can detect many pollutants in a single test, many microfluidic and biosensor-based approaches are only designed to detect a single analyte. This limits their application for comprehensive screening of numerous adulterants concurrently (Vinothkanna et al., 2024).3.Lack of standardization and regulatory barriers: The lack of global standardization for fast detection technologies impedes their use in regulatory enforcement. Studies on functional food adulteration reveal variations in the validation of novel detection systems, affecting global adoption (Hu, Zou, et al., 2024b).4.Sensitivity and Detection Limits: Rapid detection technologies, such as μPADs and electrochemical biosensors, still struggle to reach laboratory-level detection limits. In essential oil authentication, colorimetric tests exhibit larger detection limits than chromatography-based techniques, limiting their usefulness in identifying slight adulteration (Yang et al., 2024).5.Integration with digital platforms for data interpretation: While smartphone-based detection is convenient, variations in camera resolution, lighting conditions, and human interaction might cause inconsistencies. A study on egg adulteration detection discovered that smartphone photography performance varied greatly depending on the environmental circumstances (Ray et al., 2023b)6.Cost and accessibility concerns: Despite being low-cost alternatives, some microfluidic devices and portable biosensors necessitate specialized reagents and production procedures that may not be readily available in all areas. According to research on pomegranate juice authentication, pricing and accessibility continue to be major barriers to wider use.7.Industrial-Scale Implementation Challenges: Many detection systems are still in the research stage and lack scalability for real-time industrial applications. For example, research on heavy metal pollution detection utilising microfluidic platforms shows that, while promising, these systems require more improvement before mass deployment (Guan & Sun, 2020a, 2020b).8.Cross-reactivity and false positives:Biosensor-based methodologies, such as aptamer-based and immunoassay assays, might demonstrate cross-reactivity, resulting in false-positive results. In meat authenticity investigations, molecular assays occasionally misidentified species due to protein cross-reactivity (Becchi et al., 2024b)

Matrix complexity and interference issues: Many detection techniques are challenging to use because food matrices are complex and contain a variety of physical and chemical components that can interfere with analytical results. Microfluidic paper-based analytical devices (μPADs) have limited sensitivity and specificity for identifying adulterants in dairy, honey, and culinary oils due to matrix effects.

Limited multi-analyte detection capabilities: While classic techniques such as HPLC and GC–MS can detect many pollutants in a single test, many microfluidic and biosensor-based approaches are only designed to detect a single analyte. This limits their application for comprehensive screening of numerous adulterants concurrently (Vinothkanna et al., 2024).

Lack of standardization and regulatory barriers: The lack of global standardization for fast detection technologies impedes their use in regulatory enforcement. Studies on functional food adulteration reveal variations in the validation of novel detection systems, affecting global adoption (Hu, Zou, et al., 2024b).

Sensitivity and Detection Limits: Rapid detection technologies, such as μPADs and electrochemical biosensors, still struggle to reach laboratory-level detection limits. In essential oil authentication, colorimetric tests exhibit larger detection limits than chromatography-based techniques, limiting their usefulness in identifying slight adulteration (Yang et al., 2024).

Integration with digital platforms for data interpretation: While smartphone-based detection is convenient, variations in camera resolution, lighting conditions, and human interaction might cause inconsistencies. A study on egg adulteration detection discovered that smartphone photography performance varied greatly depending on the environmental circumstances (Ray et al., 2023b)

Cost and accessibility concerns: Despite being low-cost alternatives, some microfluidic devices and portable biosensors necessitate specialized reagents and production procedures that may not be readily available in all areas. According to research on pomegranate juice authentication, pricing and accessibility continue to be major barriers to wider use.

Industrial-Scale Implementation Challenges: Many detection systems are still in the research stage and lack scalability for real-time industrial applications. For example, research on heavy metal pollution detection utilising microfluidic platforms shows that, while promising, these systems require more improvement before mass deployment (Guan & Sun, 2020a, 2020b).
Cross-reactivity and false positives:

Biosensor-based methodologies, such as aptamer-based and immunoassay assays, might demonstrate cross-reactivity, resulting in false-positive results. In meat authenticity investigations, molecular assays occasionally misidentified species due to protein cross-reactivity (Becchi et al., 2024b)

The review of the existing literature shows that the main challenge for the implementation of this concept does not lie in the lack of ideas to detect food fraud, but rather in the lack of transition from concept testing to the development of validated methods. Further research needs to focus more on practical aspects such as reproducibility and shelf-life.
Future Directions to Overcome These Challenges:
Improving Multi-Analyte Detection: Advances in lab-on-a-chip technology may allow for the simultaneous detection of several adulterants, improving real-time monitoring efficiency.
Standardization and Validation: Regulatory organizations should collaborate to develop harmonized rules for rapid detection instruments to guarantee consistent and trustworthy results.
Enhancing Sensitivity Using Nanotechnology: The use of nanomaterials in biosensors can reduce detection limits, making rapid tests more competitive with traditional approaches.
AI-Driven Analysis and Automation: Machine learning models may improve pattern recognition and interpretation of results, potentially decreasing human error in digital detection systems.
Industry Adoption and Cost-Effective Scaling: Increased collaboration among researchers, food manufacturers, and regulatory bodies has the potential to hasten commercialization and reduce costs.

Nevertheless, traditional analytic methods such as chromatography, spectroscopy, and DNA analysis are highly valuable for reliable detection of fraud in food. Nonetheless, due to the need for special equipment, skilled personnel, and laboratory conditions, they are not always suitable for rapid on-site detection of food fraud. From the literature review conducted, one can conclude that the value of microfluidics in food fraud detection is based on the possibility of the integration of sample preparation and analysis into a compact, portable, and relatively cheap device. Microfluidic technologies are applied in such areas as adulterant detection, allergen screening, pathogen detection, and food authentication.

The reviewed literature provides sufficient information to make conclusion that the main advantage of microfluidic systems does not consist in replacement of laboratory techniques but in the combination with these methods and making rapid screening decisions possible in the places without conventional laboratories. Nevertheless, many applications have been proved only under experimental conditions in the case of specific matrices. Thus, future researches should focus on increasing sensitivity, selectivity, decreasing cross-reactivity, overcoming matrix effects, and proving reproducibility on diverse real-life samples. Multiplexed systems, which can detect several indicators of fraud simultaneously, may become a new trend in this field.

For implementation from an industrial point of view, issues like scalability, cost-effective manufacturing, stability of devices, testing processes, and performance of analysis should be considered. Cooperation between researchers, food industries, regulatory organizations, and technology developers will be crucial for setting up proper validation and regulation frameworks for portable food fraud detection devices.

Combining the use of microfluidics with smartphone technology, artificial intelligence, and digital traceability could help achieve rapid on-site food fraud detection and analysis. Nevertheless, the successful implementation will be based on analysis validation, reproducibility, testing protocols, regulations, and performance on actual food samples. In general, microfluidics is a promising technology for rapid and decentralized food fraud screening.
